guideTitle: 6 Best Overbed Tables With Wheels in 2026
metaTitle: Best Overbed Tables With Wheels in 2026
metaDescription: Six rolling overbed tables compared on height range, caster locks, base shape and surface size, to help you match one to your bed, chair or sofa.
introParagraphs: A rolling overbed table earns its place when a person eats, reads, writes or uses a tablet from a bed, recliner or sofa and does not want to carry a tray back and forth. The wheels are what make it a piece of furniture instead of a tray: you can park it beside the bed, slide it across, and push it clear when you stand up. That same mobility is also the main design risk, which is why the caster setup deserves as much attention as the tabletop.

This lineup covers six wheeled tables that differ in how they lift, how they roll and how much surface they offer. Two use a counterbalanced or pneumatic height mechanism, one is a classic woodgrain hospital style, one tilts through a very wide arc, one is a long bed desk with outlets, and one has a measured tabletop. Every one is a household or care-setting product, not a medical device, and none of our commentary is medical advice.

We evaluated each table based on product specs and buyer feedback, not hands-on use. If the table will support someone who leans on it to stand, or if bed clearance and floor type are unusual, an occupational or physical therapist can advise on what suits that person. Check the manufacturer's stated weight limit before relying on any table for load beyond a meal and a laptop.

products.name: Vaunn Medical Adjustable Overbed Table
products.description:
The Vaunn uses a counterbalanced hydraulic mechanism, so height changes continuously instead of clicking between fixed notches. You raise or lower the top with one hand and stop wherever the surface sits right for a meal or a book. The frame is welded tubular steel with a chrome finish, which is the sort of surface that wipes down easily.

It is built in a hospital-and-home style, so it looks more clinical than a furniture-style desk. That suits a long-term care setup but may feel out of place in a living room. Buyers who want a laptop angle will find this a flat-top design with no tilt.

Ownership is simple: roll it in, lock the wheels, and adjust. Compared with the Drive Medical at 28 inches minimum height, the Vaunn's stepless lift makes small corrections easier. Next to the DUMOS with its pneumatic lift, the Vaunn leans toward a sturdy steel look over a slimmer profile.
products.bestFor: Someone who wants smooth one-handed height changes and an easy-wipe steel frame.

Welded steel frame wipes clean quickly
Counterbalanced lift moves without much force
Works for bed, recliner or chair use
cons: Clinical look in a living room
Flat top with no tilt option for reading
Heavier than the slim pneumatic desks

products.name: Drive Medical Overbed Table, Woodgrain Top
products.description:
The Drive Medical is the traditional layout many people picture when they hear overbed table: a woodgrain top on a steel base with swivel casters. It offers a user-friendly lift that places the surface from 28 inches upward. A secure lock keeps the height where you set it.

The woodgrain surface looks warmer than bare steel and fits more naturally in a bedroom. The trade-off is that it is a fixed flat top, so reading at an angle needs a pillow or a book stand. Its lineup siblings with tilt, such as the YATINEY, solve that but add moving parts.

Day to day it behaves like a dependable basic: swivel casters let it turn quickly in tight spaces, and the lock steadies it once parked. At a 28 inch minimum it sits lower than the DUMOS at similar settings, which helps with low beds and recliners. It is a sensible choice if you want familiar parts and an easy-to-replace design.
products.bestFor: A bedroom or care setup where a familiar, furniture-friendly look matters.

products.name: DUMOS Overbed Table with Wheels, White
products.description:
The DUMOS pairs a pneumatic lift with hidden swivel casters in a slimmer, more modern shape. A squeeze or push on the control raises or lowers the surface, and the gas spring does the work. Hidden 360 degree casters keep the base lower and protect floors while rolling quietly.

The listing describes a heavy-duty steel frame and mentions up to 20 lbs of gear, so treat it as a table for a meal, a book or a laptop rather than something to lean on. That limit is the main trade-off against the sturdier Vaunn. It comes in several colors, which helps it blend into a bedroom.

In practice it is easy to slide beside a bed or chair, and its small footprint stores well along a wall. Compared with the HOOBRO, the DUMOS offers a far smaller surface but much easier maneuvering. It makes the most sense for light daily tasks where a quiet roll and a clean look matter more than load.
products.bestFor: People who want a slim, quiet table for light tasks beside a bed or sofa.

products.name: Medical King Adjustable Overbed Table
products.description:
The Medical King lists dimensions of 30 by 15.5 by 45 inches, giving a deeper tray than the narrow DUMOS desks. That space fits a plate, a drink and a book at the same time. The height is adjustable so the surface can sit at lap height or higher for seated use.

The design follows the hospital table pattern: a wide top, a rolling base, and a lift to fine tune position. Buyers get a practical surface but fewer extras, since there is no tilt, outlet or drawer. It reads as a straightforward working table.

For ownership, expect to lock the wheels before setting down a hot meal and to measure the base against the bed's clearance. Next to the Vaunn it offers a comparable footprint but less detailed lift information in the listing. Against the YATINEY at 21.7 to 35.4 inches, it targets higher bed and chair setups.
products.bestFor: Someone who mostly eats and reads from bed and wants a roomy flat top.

products.name: YATINEY Overbed Table with Wheels, Tilting Top
products.description:
The YATINEY is the lowest-reaching table here, with a height range of 21.7 to 35.4 inches. That makes it a natural fit for low sofas, recliners and lower beds where taller tables hover too high. The tabletop tilts across 0 to 180 degrees, and a slot holds a tablet or phone for reading, writing or drawing.

Four swivel casters provide movement around the room, and the lockable wheels hold it still. The wide tilt arc is helpful but brings extra moving parts to keep tight and clean. Its top is aimed at laptop and desk-style tasks more than heavy meal service.

For storage it is more compact than the HOOBRO and easier to push than the Medical King. Where the Drive Medical starts at 28 inches, the YATINEY reaches several inches lower, so it suits seating that sits closer to the floor. Check that a tilted surface does not let items slide off before leaving a drink on it.
products.bestFor: Sofa and recliner users who need a low, tilting surface for reading or a tablet.

products.name: HOOBRO Overbed Table with Outlets and Light Strip
products.description:
The HOOBRO is the largest design here, a long bed desk sized for queen beds and smaller at 70.9 by 15.3 inches. It brings a power strip with two standard outlets, a USB port and a Type-C port, plus a light strip. A drawer sits under the surface for small items.

It has four lockable wheels and four height levels, which is fewer steps than the stepless Vaunn. The build uses particleboard and metal, so it reads as furniture, not a clinical table. That makes it a good fit for working or gaming from bed rather than for care-setting meals.

Its size is also its limit: it needs real bedroom space and a clear path to roll. Compared with the DUMOS, the HOOBRO gives many times the surface at the cost of agility. Check that the base and legs clear your bed frame, and keep the cord routed so it does not become a trip hazard.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A table that rolls must also stop, so the caster locks are the first thing to check. Look for at least two locking wheels, and ideally four, as on the HOOBRO with its 4 lockable wheels or the YATINEY with 4 swivel casters. Wheels about 1.5 inches tall roll better over carpet, while very small hidden casters like those on the DUMOS suit smoother floors. If someone might lean on the table to rise, a therapist can advise whether a rolling table is appropriate at all.

The lowest and highest settings decide whether the table works with your bed, sofa or recliner. Measure the seat or mattress surface and compare it with the range, such as 28 inches upward on the Drive Medical or 21.7 to 35.4 inches on the YATINEY. A low-seating user needs a low minimum, and someone sitting up in a tall bed needs more top end. Stepless lifts like the Vaunn make fine adjustments easier than four fixed levels like the HOOBRO.

The base has to slide under or beside the bed without catching. Many beds leave only about 5 inches of clearance underneath, so a thick frame or cross bar can block it. Check the base shape in each listing, since H, C and U layouts reach differently. The long HOOBRO at 70.9 inches needs the most floor space, while the DUMOS is easiest to slip beside a chair.

A table that is too small forces you to juggle plates and devices, and one that is too big collides with furniture. The Medical King at 30 by 15.5 inches fits a plate and a book, while the HOOBRO at 70.9 by 15.3 inches spans a whole bed. Look for a raised edge or non-slip surface so items stay put when you roll the table. Remember that a depth near 15 inches is typical, so deep trays are rare.

Hydraulic, pneumatic and notched lifts feel different in use. The Vaunn offers a stepless counterbalanced lift with one hand, the DUMOS uses a pneumatic spring, and the HOOBRO moves between four set levels. A smooth lift matters most for people with limited grip strength or one usable hand. Test that the table stays at height without creeping down once loaded.

Extras help only if you will use them. Tilt on the YATINEY, which spans 0 to 180 degrees, suits reading and drawing, but moving parts need occasional tightening. Power on the HOOBRO adds convenience with its 2 outlets, USB and Type-C ports, though a cord can become a trip hazard. If you only eat and sip from the table, a plain flat top like the Drive Medical is simpler and easier to clean.

howWeEvaluated.title: Caster and stability design
howWeEvaluated.description: We read each listing for wheel count, swivel and lock details, and base shape. Tables with four lockable wheels, like the HOOBRO, scored well for staying parked. Hidden casters such as the DUMOS's 360 degree units scored for floor protection. This criterion mattered most because a rolling table has to stop reliably.

howWeEvaluated.title: Height range and lift
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated height ranges and the way each table raises. The YATINEY reaches down to 21.7 inches, the Drive Medical starts at 28 inches, and the Vaunn offers stepless adjustment. Effort to adjust counted too, since one-handed use helps people with limited grip.

howWeEvaluated.title: Surface and usability
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at tabletop size, material and any tilt or edge details. The Medical King at 30 by 15.5 inches and the HOOBRO at 70.9 by 15.3 inches sit at opposite ends. Surface features such as the YATINEY's tablet slot were weighed against added complexity.

howWeEvaluated.title: Build and cleaning
howWeEvaluated.description: We assessed frame material and how easily each table wipes down. Welded chrome-plated steel on the Vaunn is simple to clean, while the HOOBRO's particleboard and metal blend favors a home look. Moving parts like tilt hinges were treated as extra wear points.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value and lineup fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We positioned each pick against the others so no two serve the same role. The Vaunn leads on lift smoothness, the DUMOS on slimness, the HOOBRO on power and size, and the YATINEY on low seating. Based on product specs and buyer feedback, not on hands-on use.

faq.q: How many locking wheels should an overbed table have?
faq.a: At least two locking wheels is a sensible minimum, and four is better for a table that holds drinks and devices. The HOOBRO lists four lockable wheels and the YATINEY pairs four swivel casters with lockable wheels. Always lock them before setting something hot on the surface. Locks do not make a rolling table a support for standing.

faq.q: Can I lean on an overbed table to stand up?
faq.a: Treat these tables as work surfaces, not mobility supports. They roll, and their stated limits are for items placed on top, such as the DUMOS's 20 lbs of gear. Leaning on one could tip it or roll it away. An occupational or physical therapist can recommend proper standing aids for someone who needs them.

faq.q: What height should I look for?
faq.a: Match the range to your seating. The YATINEY reaches 21.7 inches for low sofas, the Drive Medical starts at 28 inches, and tall beds need a higher maximum. Measure the seat or mattress height first. A table that cannot reach lap level will force awkward reaching.

faq.q: Do wheels work on carpet and hardwood?
faq.a: Wheel size and style decide that. Larger casters of about 1.5 inches roll more easily over carpet, while small hidden casters like those on the DUMOS suit smoother floors. Thick carpet slows any caster. Test the path from bed to parking spot before deciding.

faq.q: Is a tilt top worth it?
faq.a: A tilt helps if you read, write or use a tablet, and the YATINEY offers 0 to 180 degrees with a tablet slot. It also adds moving parts that need occasional tightening. For eating and drinking a flat top like the Medical King is simpler. A tilt that is too steep can let items slide off.

faq.q: Will it fit under my bed?
faq.a: Many beds leave only around 5 inches of clearance below, so measure before buying. A table with a low, simple base slides in more easily. The HOOBRO is long, so it is better sized for the bedside than for tight corners. Check the base shape in the listing for any cross bars.

faq.q: How do I clean and maintain one?
faq.a: Wipe steel and chrome surfaces like the Vaunn with a damp cloth, and keep moisture off particleboard such as the HOOBRO's top. Check casters occasionally for hair or debris that can stop them turning. Tighten any tilt hinges if the top starts to wobble. Follow the manufacturer's care notes for the finish.
